A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same research work. Their main text, equations, figures, tables, and appendices are readable and support matching content across renumbering and relocation.

before.justification: v1 reports original CIFAR-10 experiments, synthetic classification experiments varying network width, and simulations illustrating the theoretical constructions and bound.

after.justification: v2 retains those original experiments and adds CIFAR-10 comparisons of test-loss differences and embedding similarity across representation dimensions in Appendix F.4.

M1.justification: The softmax model family, LLV distance construction, and PLS-SVD procedure are unchanged. The new df,g notation names the maximum of embedding and unembedding dissimilarities already present in v1's Theorem 4.6; it does not introduce a new procedure.

E1.justification: Both versions evaluate CIFAR-10, the same synthetic classification tasks with 4, 6, 10, and 18 classes, and constructed model comparisons. Adding representation dimensions changes model configurations within CIFAR-10, not dataset or task coverage.

E2.justification: The reported comparisons retain KL divergence, LLV distance, mCCA, and PLS-SVD-based dissimilarity. The added loss-versus-mCCA analysis introduces no new comparison method, and the newly cited shape-metrics paper is not evaluated.

E3.justification: Appendix F.3 expands CIFAR-10 representation dimensions from 2 in v1 to 2, 3, and 5 in v2, supporting new pairwise test-loss-versus-mCCA comparisons. The stated training budget remains 20,000 steps with batch size 32; the existing synthetic evaluation settings are retained.

E4.justification: New Appendix F.4 and Figure 5 examine whether differences in test loss track embedding similarity across three CIFAR-10 representation dimensions. This supplements the earlier two-dimensional examples. Existing permutation visualizations, noise-perturbation analysis, and width analyses are retained.

E5.justification: Both versions report 20-seed synthetic experiments, 10-seed CIFAR-10 experiments, and standard-deviation shading in the width plots. The additional CIFAR-10 dimensions follow the same 10-seed practice. No new confidence intervals, significance tests, or uncertainty-estimation procedure is introduced.

E6.justification: v2 adds Figure 5's pairwise loss-difference and mCCA results for dimensions 2, 3, and 5, showing that small loss differences can accompany substantial representational differences. Table 1's values and the Section 5.1 example remain unchanged, including test losses 1.19 and 1.18 and mCCA 0.55.

T1.justification: The identifiability theorem, KL counterexample, likelihood corollary, LLV assumptions, and dissimilarity bound retain their mathematical substance and appendix proofs. Definition 4.6 restates the maximum already used in v1's bound, now numbered Theorem 4.7. Weyl's inequality is reorganized rather than changed.

C1.justification: The central claims remain that small KL divergence or near-optimal likelihood need not ensure representational similarity, LLV closeness bounds representational dissimilarity, and wider networks empirically tend toward closer distributions and representations. The revised abstract and conclusion preserve these claims.

C2.justification: Section 6 explicitly distinguishes the existence of constructed counterexamples from their emergence during training. It also specifies that diversity can fail for image classifiers when label count is smaller than representation dimension. These refine the earlier discussion of learned dissimilarity and applicability restrictions.

D1.justification: v2 supplies an experimental-code repository and archival DOI in Section 5, repeats code-access information in Appendix F, and points to the repository for additional dependencies in Appendix H. v1 provided experimental settings and the upstream ResNet implementation reference but no corresponding project-code access information.

R1.justification: v2 adds Williams et al.'s Generalized shape metrics on neural representations to the introduction and references. The broader positioning relative to identifiability theory and existing representation-similarity measures remains unchanged; other bibliographic edits largely concern formatting or numbering.

P1.justification: v2 clarifies the permutation construction, equivalence-class terminology, and distinction between vector-level and model-level dissimilarity. It adds a checklist and appendix contents page and consolidates the Weyl-inequality discussion. The main narrative and appendix organization otherwise remain substantially intact.

P2.justification: v2 adds the three-panel Figure 5, expands the notation table, revises Figure 1's equivalence-class labels, and updates plot labels to df,g. Existing CIFAR-10 visualizations are retained and renumbered, with modest resizing, legend, caption, and placement changes.

improvement.justification: v2 improves clarity through more precise notation, construction explanations, and applicability qualifications. Figure 5 adds supporting evidence beyond the original two-dimensional illustration, while the repository and DOI improve reproducibility information. These gains are incremental because the central theory and primary results are unchanged. A small editorial inconsistency remains: Section 3 calls the new Appendix F.4 illustration synthetic although it uses CIFAR-10.
